reconcile.connective: Gill's Trinitarian reading resolves the tension across all four texts: 'alone' and 'by myself' in Isaiah 44:24 exclude creatures, not Trinitarian persons, while the NT passages distribute the one creative act among Father, Son, and Spirit without contradiction.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman argues that the NT's attribution of creation to Christ stands in genuine tension with the OT's strict monotheistic formula — Isaiah 44:24 declares YHWH stretched out the heavens 'alone, by myself,' a claim the later Logos-theology of John 1 and Colossians 1 cannot harmonize without altering the plain sense of the text.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, How Jesus Became God (HarperOne, 2014)

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: not to the exclusion of the Father and the Holy Spirit, but of all creatures, angels and men; of himself, and by his own strength and power, and, without the help of these, he stretched out the vast space of the heavens as a curtain, and spread out the earth in its length and breadth
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill directly addresses the 'alone/by myself' language of Isaiah 44:24, parsing it as the exclusion of creaturely agency rather than of the other Trinitarian persons — the key move that allows the verse to coexist with NT co-creator claims.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: when he is said to be the one God, it must be understood, not as exclusive of the Son and Spirit… but as dominion or lordship belongs to the Father, so deity to the Son, and also to the Spirit.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill's comment on 1 Cor 8:6 explains that the monotheistic formula does not exclude the Son from divinity or from creative agency — the Father's singular lordship and the Son's singular creative role are complementary distributions of one divine act.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: nor to the exclusion of the Father and Spirit, who, with the Son, were jointly concerned in the creating of all things out of nothing
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: On the Colossians 1:16 attribution of creation to Christ, Gill specifies that this excludes neither the Father nor the Spirit — establishing that the NT co-creator formula and the OT YHWH-alone formula both refer to the undivided act of the one Triune God.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the question of creation attributed both to YHWH alone (Isaiah 44:24) and to Christ (John 1, Colossians 1), defending the Trinitarian harmonization that 'alone' excludes creaturely participation rather than other divine persons.
